title: API returns intermittent 503 responses while CPU remains low
description: Diagnose intermittent 503 Service Unavailable responses with low CPU by investigating connection pools, thread pools, health checks, and upstream rate limiting.

data.text: Your API returns 503 errors for about 2% of requests, but CPU and memory usage are well below capacity. The errors appear in bursts and then disappear. This pattern points away from resource exhaustion and toward transient infrastructure issues: connection pool exhaustion, thread pool starvation, health check failures, or upstream rate limiting.

items: Database connection pool is exhausted during traffic spikes, and new requests wait until timeout
Thread pool is saturated by blocking I/O calls, causing request queueing and eventual timeouts
Load balancer health checks are failing intermittently, removing healthy instances from rotation
Upstream API gateway is rate limiting based on a burst threshold
DNS resolution is timing out for a dependency, and the fallback path is also failing
A background task is holding a shared lock, blocking request threads for seconds at a time

terms.definition: HTTP status code indicating the server is temporarily unable to handle the request, often due to overload or maintenance.
All connections in a pool are in use, so new requests wait or fail until a connection is returned.
All worker threads are blocked, so new requests queue indefinitely and time out.
An automated probe that verifies an instance is healthy before routing traffic to it.
Restricting the number of requests a client can make in a given time window.

items: Check load balancer and API gateway metrics for 503 counts and upstream response codes
Correlate 503 timestamps with connection pool usage metrics from your APM tool
Inspect thread pool queue depth and active thread counts during the burst window
Review health check logs for intermittent failures on the affected instances
Check for upstream rate limit headers (X-RateLimit-Remaining) in failed request logs
Look for blocking calls in recent deployments using profiling or flame graphs

cards.title: Connection pool exhaustion
cards.description: All DB connections are in use; new requests timeout waiting.
pros: Easy to monitor with pool metrics
cons: Can be caused by connection leaks
Tuning pool size alone may not fix it

cards.title: Thread pool starvation
cards.description: All threads blocked on I/O; request queue grows until timeout.

cards.title: Health check flapping
cards.description: Instance is healthy but health check fails intermittently.
pros: Health checks are usually simple to fix

cards.title: Upstream rate limiting
cards.description: Gateway or CDN rejects requests after a threshold.
pros: External cause is easy to confirm from headers

data.title: Thread pool saturation evidence
data.content: A thread dump showing most threads blocked on a downstream call:
data.code:
"pool-1-thread-3" #12 waiting on condition
    at java.lang.Object.wait(Native Method)
    at com.example.PaymentClient.charge(PaymentClient.java:45)
    - waiting on <0x1a2b3c4d> (a java.util.concurrent.FutureTask)

"pool-1-thread-4" #13 waiting on condition
    at java.lang.Object.wait(Native Method)
    at com.example.PaymentClient.charge(PaymentClient.java:45)
    - waiting on <0x1a2b3c4e> (a java.util.concurrent.FutureTask)

... 48 of 50 threads in same blocked state

data.caption: Diagnostic flow for intermittent 503s with low CPU

data.title: 503 is a symptom, not a root cause
data.text: Do not assume the API itself is broken. In microservice architectures, 503s often originate from a downstream dependency. Follow the chain outward: load balancer, API gateway, service mesh, and finally the application.

data.title: Diagnose a 503 storm from metrics
data.description: You are given a set of dashboards showing CPU, connection pool usage, thread pool queue depth, and 503 rate over a 30-minute window. Identify the root cause and write a remediation plan.
steps: Plot 503 rate against connection pool utilization
Plot 503 rate against thread pool queue depth
Identify the metric that correlates most strongly with 503s
Trace the root cause to a specific code path or configuration
Write a remediation plan with immediate and long-term fixes
data.expectedOutcome: You should be able to distinguish between connection pool exhaustion, thread pool starvation, and upstream rate limiting using only metric correlations.

data.title: Summary
points: Low CPU with 503s points to I/O bottlenecks, not compute
Correlate 503s with connection pool and thread pool metrics
Check health checks and upstream rate limits before changing application code
Use thread dumps and APM profiling to find blocking calls
data.takeaway: The fastest fix is not always in the application layer. Look at the full request path, including load balancers and upstream services.
